exact_claim: Strasbourg, July 1518: a dancing epidemic lasting into late August/September
Began with Frau Troffea on about 14 July, dancing alone without music
She danced for 4-6 days; her husband begged her to stop
Within days, more than thirty people were dancing
One chronicle counted 400 afflicted within a month
Frau Troffea was taken to the shrine of St. Vitus (Saverne)
Physicians: 'a natural disease, which comes from overheated blood'; prescribed dancing it out
Council converted guild halls, built stages in the horse and grain markets, hired musicians (drums, pipes, horns) and strong men to hold dancers up
Stages pulled down; public music and dancing banned until September; at weddings only strings, no tambourines or drums
Worst cases sent by wagon to St. Vitus shrine; red shoes, crosses, holy water

notes: Only as: later chronicles claimed it; the city's records of the time don't mention deaths

exact_claim: Cause unknown; one leading interpretation is stress-induced mass psychogenic illness; the ergot theory is contested
More than ten dancing outbreaks along the Rhine and Moselle since 1374
Paracelsus claimed Troffea danced to annoy her husband
notes: Humour beat; flag as his opinion
